questions.stem: The nurse on a cardiac step-down unit receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?

options.text: A client with heart failure whose weight is 0.5 kg (1.1 lb) higher than yesterday
A client 4 hours after a femoral cardiac catheterization who reports new low back pain; heart rate 118/min, blood pressure 88/56 mm Hg
A client with atrial fibrillation taking warfarin whose INR this morning is 2.8
A client with stable angina who asks for sublingual nitroglycerin before walking in the hall

rationale.correct: New back pain with tachycardia and hypotension after femoral access suggests a retroperitoneal bleed, which is a life-threatening hemorrhage that may show no visible groin hematoma.

perOption.a: A 0.5 kg overnight gain is below the usual reporting threshold (about 1 to 1.5 kg in a day or 2 kg in a week); it needs monitoring, not immediate action.
perOption.b: Back or flank pain plus signs of hypovolemic shock after femoral catheterization indicates retroperitoneal bleeding; this client is unstable.
perOption.c: An INR of 2.8 is within the usual therapeutic range (2 to 3) for atrial fibrillation.
perOption.d: Taking nitroglycerin before exertion is an appropriate, planned use; the client is stable.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize retroperitoneal bleeding as the priority after femoral cardiac catheterization.

questions.stem: A client in the emergency department reports crushing substernal chest pain. Blood pressure is 132/84 mm Hg. During the medication history the client states, "I took sildenafil last night." Which prescription should the nurse clarify with the provider before giving it?

options.text: Aspirin 324 mg chewed now
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg sublingual every 5 minutes, up to 3 doses
12-lead ECG now
Troponin level now and in 3 hours

rationale.correct: Nitrates taken within 24 hours of sildenafil (48 hours for tadalafil) can cause severe, refractory hypotension, so the nitroglycerin order must be clarified.

perOption.a: Chewed aspirin reduces platelet aggregation and is indicated early in suspected acute coronary syndrome.
perOption.b: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors potentiate the vasodilating effect of nitrates and can cause profound hypotension.
perOption.c: A 12-lead ECG should be obtained within 10 minutes of arrival with chest pain.
perOption.d: Serial troponin levels are needed to confirm or rule out myocardial infarction.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: Review the exhibit, then complete the sentence.

content.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {{b1}} myocardial infarction, so the nurse should monitor closely for {{b2}}.

options.text: an anterior
an inferior
a lateral
bradycardia and heart block
hypertensive crisis
hyperkalemia

rationale.correct: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF shows an inferior MI, usually from right coronary artery occlusion. That artery commonly supplies the SA and AV nodes, so bradycardia and AV blocks are common.

perOption.b1:a: An anterior MI shows ST elevation in V1 to V4.
perOption.b1:b: Leads II, III and aVF look at the inferior wall.
perOption.b1:c: A lateral MI shows ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6.
perOption.b2:a: Right coronary artery occlusion often affects the SA and AV nodes, causing bradycardia and heart blocks.
perOption.b2:b: MI more often lowers blood pressure; an inferior MI with right ventricular involvement especially causes hypotension.
perOption.b2:c: Hyperkalemia is not a typical complication of the infarct location.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client is receiving a continuous IV heparin infusion for a deep vein thrombosis. The 06:00 aPTT is 122 seconds (therapeutic range per protocol: 60 to 85 seconds). The client has no signs of bleeding. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Continue the infusion and recheck the aPTT in 6 hours
Stop the infusion and follow the heparin protocol or notify the provider
Give vitamin K 10 mg subcutaneously
Increase the infusion rate by 2 units/kg/hr

rationale.correct: An aPTT well above the therapeutic range means a high bleeding risk; the infusion is held and adjusted per protocol or provider order.

perOption.a: Continuing an infusion with a supratherapeutic aPTT exposes the client to bleeding for 6 more hours.
perOption.b: Heparin protocols direct the nurse to hold the infusion for a time and then restart at a lower rate when the aPTT is too high.
perOption.c: Vitamin K reverses warfarin, not heparin; the antidote for heparin is protamine sulfate.
perOption.d: Increasing the rate would raise the aPTT even further.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Hold heparin when the aPTT is above the therapeutic range and follow the protocol.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is going home on warfarin. Which client statements show correct understanding? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I will keep the amount of green leafy vegetables I eat about the same each week."
"I will use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor."
"I will call my provider if my stools turn black or tarry."
"I can take aspirin for a headache."
"If I miss a dose, I will take two tablets the next day."
"I will tell my dentist that I take warfarin."

rationale.correct: Safe warfarin use means consistent vitamin K intake, bleeding precautions, reporting signs of bleeding and telling every provider about the drug.

perOption.a: Consistent (not zero) vitamin K intake keeps the INR stable.
perOption.b: A soft toothbrush and electric razor reduce gum and skin bleeding.
perOption.c: Black, tarry stools can signal gastrointestinal bleeding.
perOption.d: Aspirin adds antiplatelet effect and raises bleeding risk; acetaminophen is usually preferred.
perOption.e: Doubling a dose can make the INR dangerously high; the client should follow the provider's missed-dose instructions.
perOption.f: Dentists need to know so they can plan for bleeding risk before procedures.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Evaluate understanding of warfarin safety teaching.

questions.stem: A client taking digoxin 0.125 mg daily and furosemide 40 mg daily reports loss of appetite, nausea and seeing yellow-green halos around lights. Which laboratory result is most likely contributing to these findings?

options.text: Potassium 3.1 mEq/L
Sodium 138 mEq/L
Calcium 9.2 mg/dL
Magnesium 2.0 mg/dL

rationale.correct: The client has signs of digoxin toxicity. Hypokalemia, common with loop diuretics, increases digoxin's binding to the sodium-potassium pump and raises the risk of toxicity.

perOption.a: A low potassium level from furosemide increases sensitivity to digoxin and the risk of toxicity and dysrhythmias.
perOption.b: This sodium level is normal.
perOption.c: This calcium level is normal; high calcium, not normal calcium, would increase toxicity risk.
perOption.d: This magnesium level is normal; low magnesium would increase toxicity risk.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize digoxin toxicity and hypokalemia as a risk factor.

questions.stem: A client who weighs 80 kg is prescribed a heparin infusion at 18 units/kg/hr. The pharmacy supplies heparin 25,000 units in 250 mL of D5W. At what rate should the nurse set the infusion pump? Round to the nearest tenth.

rationale.correct: Dose: 18 units/kg/hr × 80 kg = 1,440 units/hr. Concentration: 25,000 units ÷ 250 mL = 100 units/mL. Rate: 1,440 ÷ 100 = 14.4 mL/hr.
references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: The nurse finds an adult client unresponsive in a hallway. Place the nurse's actions in order.

items.text: Attach the AED pads to the client's bare chest
Check responsiveness and call for help and an AED
Resume chest compressions immediately after the shock
Check for breathing and a carotid pulse for no more than 10 seconds
Make sure no one is touching the client and deliver the advised shock
Begin chest compressions at 100 to 120 per minute

rationale.correct: Recognize the arrest and activate help, confirm no pulse, start compressions, use the AED as soon as it arrives, then resume compressions right away.

perOption.a: Activating the emergency response early brings the AED and the team.
perOption.b: The pulse and breathing check is brief so compressions are not delayed.
perOption.c: High-quality compressions maintain blood flow to the brain and heart until defibrillation.
perOption.d: The AED is applied as soon as it is available.
perOption.e: Everyone must be clear of the client before the shock to prevent injury.
perOption.f: Compressions resume immediately; rhythm is not rechecked until 2 minutes of CPR are done.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Perform adult BLS with an AED in the correct order.

questions.stem: A client's cardiac monitor shows monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 180/min. The client has a palpable pulse but is confused and pale, with a blood pressure of 72/40 mm Hg. Which intervention should the nurse prepare for first?

options.text: Unsynchronized defibrillation
Synchronized cardioversion
Starting chest compressions
IV adenosine 6 mg rapid push

rationale.correct: Ventricular tachycardia with a pulse and signs of instability (hypotension, altered mental status) is treated with synchronized cardioversion.

perOption.a: Unsynchronized defibrillation is for pulseless VT or ventricular fibrillation.
perOption.b: Synchronizing the shock with the QRS avoids delivering it during the T wave and causing ventricular fibrillation.
perOption.c: Compressions are for a client without a pulse; this client has one.
perOption.d: Adenosine treats regular narrow-complex supraventricular tachycardia, not unstable VT.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Choose synchronized cardioversion for unstable tachycardia with a pulse.

questions.stem: A client has had atrial fibrillation for an unknown length of time and is not taking an anticoagulant. Elective cardioversion is planned. Which test should the nurse expect to be done before the cardioversion?

options.text: Transesophageal echocardiogram
Exercise stress test
Pulmonary function tests
Holter monitoring for 48 hours

rationale.correct: Atrial fibrillation lasting 48 hours or more (or of unknown duration) can form clots in the left atrium. Cardioversion can dislodge them, so a TEE is done to rule out thrombus, or the client is anticoagulated for about 3 weeks first.

perOption.a: A TEE gives a clear view of the left atrial appendage, where clots usually form.
perOption.b: A stress test evaluates ischemia, not atrial clots, and is unsafe for an unstable rhythm.
perOption.c: Pulmonary function tests do not affect the safety of cardioversion.
perOption.d: The rhythm is already known; prolonged monitoring does not reduce the stroke risk.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Prevent stroke before cardioversion of atrial fibrillation of unknown duration.

questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it is more consistent with peripheral arterial disease or chronic venous insufficiency.

rows.text: Calf pain while walking that goes away with rest
Brownish discoloration of the skin around the ankles
Thin, shiny, hairless skin on the lower legs
Shallow ulcer with irregular edges near the medial malleolus
Pain that eases when the legs hang over the side of the bed
Pitting edema of the lower legs

rationale.correct: Arterial disease starves tissue of blood (pain, pallor, hair loss, relief with dependency). Venous disease pools blood in the legs (edema, brown staining, medial ankle ulcers).

perOption.r1:c1: Intermittent claudication comes from muscle ischemia when arterial flow can't meet demand.
perOption.r1:c2: Venous insufficiency causes aching and heaviness, not exercise-induced pain relieved by rest.
perOption.r2:c1: Arterial disease causes pallor or dependent rubor, not brown staining.
perOption.r2:c2: Hemosiderin deposits from pooled red cells stain the skin brown.
perOption.r3:c1: Chronic poor arterial flow leads to thin, shiny, hairless skin.
perOption.r3:c2: Venous disease thickens and discolors the skin rather than causing hair loss.
perOption.r4:c1: Arterial ulcers are deep, round and on the toes or pressure points.
perOption.r4:c2: Venous ulcers are shallow, irregular and near the medial malleolus.
perOption.r5:c1: Gravity improves arterial flow, so dangling the legs relieves ischemic pain.
perOption.r5:c2: Venous symptoms improve with elevation, not dependency.
perOption.r6:c1: Edema is not a typical feature of arterial disease.
perOption.r6:c2: Raised venous pressure pushes fluid into the tissues, causing edema.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell peripheral arterial disease from venous insufficiency by assessment findings.

questions.stem: A client is 2 days postoperative after a total hip replacement. The client suddenly says, "I can't catch my breath." Select the 4 findings that are most consistent with a pulmonary embolism.

options.text: Sharp chest pain that worsens on inspiration
Heart rate 124/min
SpO2 86% on room air
States "I feel like something terrible is about to happen"
Heart rate 52/min
Productive cough with thick yellow sputum for 3 days
Temperature 38.9 °C (102 °F) with chills

rationale.correct: Sudden dyspnea after orthopedic surgery, with pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia and a sense of doom, is the classic presentation of pulmonary embolism.

perOption.a: Pleuritic chest pain occurs when the embolism causes pleural irritation or infarction.
perOption.b: Tachycardia is the most common sign as the heart compensates for hypoxemia.
perOption.c: Blocked perfusion creates a ventilation-perfusion mismatch and hypoxemia.
perOption.d: Anxiety and a sense of impending doom are common with an acute PE.
perOption.e: PE usually causes tachycardia, not bradycardia.
perOption.f: A cough with purulent sputum developing over days suggests pneumonia.
perOption.g: High fever with chills points to infection rather than an acute embolism.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the signs of pulmonary embolism after orthopedic surgery.

questions.stem: A client 2 days after hip replacement suddenly develops dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain and an SpO2 of 86%. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Prepare the client for a CT pulmonary angiogram
Raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen
Obtain a prescription for a heparin bolus
Draw a D-dimer level

rationale.correct: Treat the airway and breathing problem first: positioning upright and giving oxygen improve oxygenation while the nurse calls the rapid response team and diagnostics and anticoagulation follow.

perOption.a: Diagnosis is needed, but not before correcting severe hypoxemia.
perOption.b: Sitting upright eases breathing, and oxygen treats the hypoxemia right away.
perOption.c: Anticoagulation prevents clot extension but does not fix the immediate hypoxemia.
perOption.d: D-dimer is a screening test; it does not help a client who is already hypoxic.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Address oxygenation first in a suspected pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: A client started lisinopril 10 mg daily 3 weeks ago for hypertension. Which report from the client needs immediate action by the nurse?

options.text: "I've had a dry, tickly cough for a week."
"I feel a little dizzy when I stand up quickly."
"My lips and tongue started swelling this morning."
"My lab report says my potassium is 5.0."

rationale.correct: Angioedema is a rare but life-threatening ACE inhibitor reaction that can obstruct the airway; it can occur at any time during therapy.

perOption.a: A dry cough is a common ACE inhibitor side effect; it should be reported, but it is not an emergency.
perOption.b: Orthostatic dizziness is expected early on; the client should rise slowly.
perOption.c: Lip and tongue swelling can progress to airway obstruction and needs emergency care; the drug is stopped permanently.
perOption.d: ACE inhibitors raise potassium; 5.0 mEq/L is at the upper limit of normal and needs monitoring.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize angioedema as the priority ACE inhibitor adverse effect.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client newly diagnosed with primary hypertension about lifestyle changes. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Limit sodium intake to less than 2,300 mg per day
Aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity each week
Stop the blood pressure medication once your readings are normal
Eat more fruits, vegetables and low-fat dairy products
Limit alcohol to no more than 1 drink a day for women or 2 for men
Stop smoking

rationale.correct: DASH-style eating, sodium restriction, regular exercise, limited alcohol and not smoking all lower blood pressure and cardiovascular risk.

perOption.a: Less sodium reduces fluid retention and blood pressure; 1,500 mg per day is ideal for many adults.
perOption.b: Regular aerobic exercise lowers systolic pressure.
perOption.c: Normal readings usually mean the medication is working; stopping it can cause rebound hypertension.
perOption.d: The DASH diet is rich in potassium, calcium and magnesium, which lower blood pressure.
perOption.e: Heavy alcohol intake raises blood pressure.
perOption.f: Nicotine causes vasoconstriction and speeds up atherosclerosis.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach lifestyle changes that lower blood pressure.

questions.stem: A client with heart failure is due for furosemide 40 mg IV. This morning's potassium level is 3.2 mEq/L. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Give the furosemide and recheck the potassium tomorrow
Give the furosemide with a glass of orange juice
Hold the furosemide and contact the provider about the potassium level
Give the furosemide and ask for a low-sodium diet

rationale.correct: Furosemide wastes potassium. Giving it with a potassium of 3.2 mEq/L risks worse hypokalemia and dysrhythmias, so the nurse contacts the provider before giving it (for example, for potassium replacement).

perOption.a: Waiting a day risks dangerous hypokalemia and dysrhythmias.
perOption.b: Orange juice can't correct a significant deficit before an IV loop diuretic takes effect.
perOption.c: The provider needs to decide whether to replace potassium or change the dose before more potassium is lost.
perOption.d: Restricting sodium is reasonable in heart failure but ignores the low potassium.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Check the potassium level before giving a loop diuretic.

questions.stem: One hour after a cardiac catheterization through the right femoral artery, the client says, "My groin feels warm and wet." The nurse finds bright red blood on the dressing. What is the nurse's first action?

options.text: Apply firm manual pressure just above the puncture site
Notify the provider
Check the right pedal pulses
Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees

rationale.correct: Active arterial bleeding is controlled first with direct pressure just above (proximal to) the puncture site; then the nurse calls for help and reassesses.

perOption.a: Direct pressure over the arterial puncture stops the bleeding and is the immediate priority.
perOption.b: The provider is notified, but only after the bleeding is controlled.
perOption.c: Pulses are checked after bleeding is controlled to assess circulation to the leg.
perOption.d: Flexing the hip can increase bleeding at the femoral site; the leg is kept straight.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Control femoral access-site bleeding with direct pressure first.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for a client with a known 5.8 cm abdominal aortic aneurysm. Which finding needs immediate action?

options.text: A pulsating mass felt in the periumbilical area
A bruit heard over the abdominal aorta
Sudden severe back pain with a blood pressure of 86/50 mm Hg
Blood pressure 138/86 mm Hg

rationale.correct: Sudden severe back or flank pain with hypotension signals rupture or impending rupture of the aneurysm, which is a surgical emergency.

perOption.a: A pulsatile abdominal mass is an expected finding with a large AAA (and should not be palpated deeply).
perOption.b: A bruit is an expected finding from turbulent flow through the aneurysm.
perOption.c: Back pain plus shock indicates rupture with hemorrhage.
perOption.d: Blood pressure should be kept controlled, but this reading is not an emergency.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize the signs of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm.

questions.stem: A client taking atorvastatin 40 mg daily calls the clinic. Which statement should the nurse report to the provider right away?

options.text: "I take my pill in the evening."
"My muscles have been aching and weak, and my urine looks dark."
"I'm following a low-fat diet."
"I sometimes have mild constipation."

rationale.correct: Muscle pain and weakness with dark urine suggest rhabdomyolysis, a serious statin adverse effect that can cause acute kidney injury.

perOption.a: Evening dosing is appropriate because cholesterol synthesis is highest at night.
perOption.b: Myopathy with dark urine (myoglobinuria) suggests rhabdomyolysis and needs prompt evaluation of the creatine kinase level.
perOption.c: A low-fat diet supports statin therapy.
perOption.d: Mild gastrointestinal effects are common and not urgent.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize signs of statin-induced rhabdomyolysis.

questions.stem: The charge nurse on a cardiac unit is making assignments. Which client is most appropriate to assign to a licensed practical nurse (LPN)?

options.text: A client just admitted with chest pain whose troponin result is pending
A client with chronic, stable heart failure who needs scheduled oral medications and a daily weight
A client who returned from a cardiac catheterization 30 minutes ago
A client who needs discharge teaching about a new anticoagulant

rationale.correct: LPNs care for stable clients with predictable outcomes. Initial assessments, unstable clients and new teaching stay with the RN.

perOption.a: A new admission with possible acute coronary syndrome is unstable and needs RN assessment.
perOption.b: A stable client with routine care and predictable outcomes is within the LPN's scope.
perOption.c: The early post-procedure period carries risks of bleeding and dysrhythmias that need frequent RN assessment.
perOption.d: Initial discharge teaching is an RN responsibility.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Assign stable clients with predictable outcomes to the LPN.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes is scheduled for a cardiac catheterization with contrast dye tomorrow. Which medication in the client's history should the nurse report to the provider before the procedure?

options.text: Metformin
Atorvastatin
Aspirin
Omeprazole

rationale.correct: Contrast can impair kidney function; metformin is held per protocol and restarted after kidney function is confirmed (usually after 48 hours).

perOption.a: Metformin is usually held around iodinated contrast procedures because contrast-induced kidney injury can lead to metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis.
perOption.b: Statins don't interact with contrast dye.
perOption.c: Aspirin is usually continued before cardiac catheterization.
perOption.d: Omeprazole doesn't affect contrast safety.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client has returned from a cardiac catheterization through the right femoral artery. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the right leg straight for the prescribed time
Check the pulses, color and temperature of the right foot
Check the puncture site for bleeding or hematoma
Encourage oral fluids unless restricted
Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees right away
Encourage walking within the first hour

rationale.correct: After femoral access: keep the leg straight, check the site and distal circulation, encourage fluids and limit hip flexion.

perOption.a: Keeping the leg straight prevents bleeding at the arterial puncture.
perOption.b: Distal checks detect arterial occlusion or a thrombus.
perOption.c: Bleeding is the most common complication.
perOption.d: Fluids help flush the contrast and protect the kidneys.
perOption.e: Sharp hip flexion can cause bleeding; the head of the bed is usually kept low (30 degrees or less) at first.
perOption.f: Bed rest is needed for several hours after femoral access.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: The cardiac monitor shows a regular ventricular rate of 75/min with sawtooth-shaped waves between the QRS complexes and a 4:1 conduction ratio. How should the nurse interpret this rhythm?

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
Atrial flutter
Ventricular tachycardia
Sinus rhythm with premature atrial contractions

rationale.correct: Atrial flutter: sawtooth flutter waves, often with a regular ventricular response.

perOption.a: Atrial fibrillation shows chaotic, wavy baseline activity and an irregularly irregular rhythm.
perOption.b: Sawtooth flutter waves with a fixed conduction ratio are typical of atrial flutter.
perOption.c: VT has wide QRS complexes at a fast rate.
perOption.d: Sinus rhythm has one upright P wave before each QRS.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify atrial flutter on a rhythm strip.

questions.stem: A client's heart rate is 38/min in sinus bradycardia. The client is dizzy and pale, with a blood pressure of 78/44 mm Hg. Which medication should the nurse prepare to give first?

options.text: Atropine 1 mg IV
Adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push
Metoprolol 5 mg IV
Amiodarone 150 mg IV

rationale.correct: Symptomatic bradycardia: atropine 1 mg IV (repeat every 3 to 5 minutes, up to 3 mg). If it isn't effective, use transcutaneous pacing or dopamine or epinephrine infusions.

perOption.a: Atropine is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia.
perOption.b: Adenosine slows conduction and is used for supraventricular tachycardia.
perOption.c: A beta-blocker would slow the heart rate further.
perOption.d: Amiodarone treats tachydysrhythmias.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Treat symptomatic bradycardia.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who had a permanent pacemaker inserted yesterday. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll avoid raising my arm on the pacemaker side above my shoulder for a few weeks."
"I'll carry my pacemaker identification card."
"I'll keep my cell phone in the shirt pocket over my pacemaker."
"I'll check my pulse and report it if it's below the set rate."

rationale.correct: Pacemaker teaching: limit arm movement on that side early, carry the ID card, keep magnets and phones away from the device and check the pulse.

perOption.a: Limiting arm movement keeps the new leads from moving out of place.
perOption.b: The card informs providers and security staff.
